title: radial-gradient vs linear-gradient
claim: Antipattern #17 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: 'gradients (especially radial/conic) repainted every frame on animated elements.' gradient-clip-baked already showed a live linear gradient plus clip-path is dramatically more expensive than a texture (15.09x Paint at 300). This case asks the narrower question the advice actually turns on: whether the gradient TYPE matters, or whether a gradient is a gradient.
result: NOT CONFIRMED. No reliable difference at 30, 100 or 300 elements on any phase. The web advice singles out radial gradients as expensive; in cohtml a radial gradient costs what a linear one costs. Note this does NOT contradict gradient-clip-baked, which found a live gradient 15.09x a baked texture in Paint - a gradient is expensive, but which gradient function you choose is free.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. Both gradient functions are supported; radial-gradient is listed as partial only because of the two-position 'double stop' colour-stop shorthand, which this case avoids by using two plain stops. Rule 1: one variable, the gradient function. Rule 2: identical DOM and geometry; both variants set background-image, only the function differs. Rule 3: identical JS, byte-for-byte. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the shared root-nudge damage driver, identical in both. Rule 7: no randomness. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Paint, with GPU plausible depending on whether the engine rasterises gradients on the CPU or evaluates them per-pixel on the GPU - and which of the two moves is itself the informative part of the answer. APPEARANCE NOTE: the two gradients cover the same pixels with the same colour range; only the interpolation geometry differs, which is the variable.
